findings.headline: Staff capacity diverted to Museum of Aberdeenshire capital project is slowing resolution of audit findings
findings.detail: The service attributes slow progress addressing audit issues to competing priorities and staff resourcing constraints while resources are committed to the Museum of Aberdeenshire capital project (scheduled to open 2028). As of audit in March 2026, three loans were due to expire in May 2026 but lenders had not been contacted as required by policy.
findings.matters: Staff capacity constraints around a major capital project may indicate competing demand on management bandwidth, potentially affecting both project delivery and control framework oversight.
findings.figures: Service staffing 9.5 FTE (one seasonal, one project lead for Local Regeneration Fund), Museum of Aberdeenshire project scheduled 2028
findings.quote: Staff are reporting that progress has been slow addressing these issues due to competing priorities

findings.headline: 70% of loans out have expired agreements; 92% lack insurance documentation; 84% lack annual condition reports
findings.detail: Audit testing of 13 loans out found: 9 (70%) have expired agreements, 12 (92%) lack required insurance documentation, and 11 (84%) lack annual condition reports and site visits. Two loans were approved by staff without delegated authority. Items loaned to external venues have not been maintained on loan lists since 2021 and lack insurance coverage.
findings.matters: Uninsured loaned items and expired agreements create unmitigated financial and cultural loss risk; control failures mean items may be damaged, lost, or stolen with no recovery mechanism.
findings.figures: 9 of 13 loans out expired (70%), 12 of 13 lack insurance (92%), 11 of 13 lack condition reports (84%)
findings.quote: Nine (70%) of 13 loan agreements had expired; 12 (92%) lacked insurance documentation; and 11 (84%) lacked annual condition reports and a site visit.

findings.headline: Accreditation expires 31 August 2026 with re-submission due September 2026, while audit identified multiple gaps in required governance policies
findings.detail: The museums face immediate re-accreditation submission deadline. Audit found key required documents are either outdated, missing, or not formally approved, including the Forward Plan, Collections Care and Conservation Policy, Documentation Plan, and Access Plan. These gaps must be resolved within weeks to maintain accreditation status.
findings.matters: Loss of accreditation would damage council reputation, impact grant funding eligibility, and signal inability to meet professional standards; the tight timeline creates execution risk.
findings.figures: Accredited until 31 August 2026, re-accreditation due September 2026
findings.quote: remains accredited until 31 August 2026, with its next re-accreditation submission due in September 2026

findings.headline: Only 10% of an estimated 250,000 museum items are recorded in the asset database, with 41% of high-value items sampled missing from records
findings.detail: The museum asset database contains records for only 25,144 of approximately 250,000 estimated items. Audit testing found 41% of high-value items sampled unrecorded, 10% of sampled items with incorrect location data, 33% of physically located items absent from the database, and no regular stocktakes undertaken. The service is working through a 40-year documentation backlog.
findings.matters: Undocumented collections represent unquantified financial and cultural asset loss exposure; items are at risk of theft, loss, or deterioration without proper tracking and control.
findings.figures: 10% recorded (25,144 of ~250,000), 41% of high-value items not on database, 33% of reviewed items physically present but absent from database
findings.quote: nine (41%) of these high value items were not recorded on the Museum Asset Database.

findings.headline: Void property turnaround delays are reducing rental income and straining temporary accommodation capacity
findings.detail: The council identifies delays in re-letting void properties as an ongoing operational risk. This creates compounded pressure: each void period loses rental income while simultaneously increasing demand on temporary accommodation services that are already strained by housing pressure and resettlement commitments.
findings.matters: Rental income is core housing revenue. Void delays are a controllable operational risk; their persistence suggests underlying service delivery or market issues requiring resolution.
findings.figures: No specific volumes or income loss quantified
findings.quote: Void turnaround delays: Delays in re-letting void properties can reduce rental income and increase pressure on temporary accommodation.

findings.headline: Leisure membership income is dependent on sustained capital investment and effective pricing discipline
findings.detail: The council identifies explicit risk that failure to continue investing in gym and exercise facilities would reduce income generation and compromise budget expectations. It also flags a separate risk that pricing is not managed effectively, which could weaken yield management, suggesting prior underperformance in commercial discipline.
findings.matters: Leisure income is discretionary and relies on both capital allocation and pricing decisions. Underperformance would require offsetting savings elsewhere. The pricing risk suggests this is an area of prior financial underperformance.
findings.figures: Membership growth in 2024/25 demonstrated investment return; no projection of future income provided
findings.quote: Leisure membership product: Failure to continue investing in the core membership offer, including gyms and group exercise, could reduce income generation potential and affect delivery of budget expectations. There is also a risk that pricing is not managed effectively, which could weaken yield management and undervalue the product offered.

findings.headline: 11.2% of planned savings (£150k) are flagged as at risk of not being achieved this financial year
findings.detail: Of £1.341m total savings agreed across Communities Committee functions, only £0.457m (34%) have been realised to date, £0.734m (54.7%) are on track, but £0.150m (11.2%) are marked amber and at risk of delivery. Non-achievement would require compensating reductions or reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: Budget delivery depends on saving plans maturing. At Q1, 11% of the savings target remains unresolved; any slippage reduces headroom to manage other operational pressures.
findings.figures: £0.150m at amber status; £1.341m total savings target
findings.quote: Savings at risk of not being achieved this financial year (Amber): £0.150m (11.2% of target)

findings.headline: Continued pressure on housing supply is compromising the council's ability to accommodate people experiencing homelessness
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies a housing emergency as an operational risk that threatens its statutory duty. Delays in void property turnaround and pressure from resettlement schemes are reducing rental income and straining temporary accommodation capacity. The council states it is maintaining services through new build activity and homelessness options work, but acknowledges the risk remains unresolved.
findings.matters: Inability to meet statutory homelessness duties would constitute a governance failure. Rising pressure on temporary accommodation also indicates growing revenue cost exposure not yet reflected in budget.
findings.figures: Housing emergency identified as material risk; no quantified cost impact provided
findings.quote: Housing emergency: Continued pressure on housing supply may compromise the Council's ability to accommodate people experiencing homelessness and meet wider housing need.

findings.headline: Registered risk: resources may be insufficient to meet statutory duties and requirements
findings.detail: IJB Risk 3629 is that resources provided are insufficient to meet statutory duties, standards and requirements. This remains unresolved on the risk register and reflects the baseline financial adequacy concern for a health and social care partnership.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the organisation has a documented risk that it may lack resources to meet statutory obligations—a governance and delivery risk.
findings.figures: Risk 3629 (active)
findings.quote: IJB Risk 3629 – The risk is that resources provided are insufficient to meet statutory duties, standards and requirements.

findings.headline: Underlying financial challenges persist despite improved 2025/26 outturn
findings.detail: The paper emphasises that the transition from recovery framework should not be read as challenges being resolved. The position has only stabilised sufficiently to move to routine governance. Focus for 2026/27 must remain on maintaining financial discipline, and the forecast position remains subject to change pending final severance figures and other in-year movements.
findings.matters: The IJB's structural financial sustainability remains uncertain. The improved position reflects underbudget management and one-off funding, not underlying service/demand sustainability.
findings.figures: 2025/26 underwriting required £3.147m of £17.155m assumed; 2026/27 forecast only £358k underbudget
findings.quote: The transition from the Recovery Plan should therefore not be interpreted as meaning that the IJB's financial challenges have been resolved; rather, the position has stabilised sufficiently to apply the same level of grip and discipline through routine reporting, escalation and decision-making arrangements.

findings.headline: £8.0m General Reserve is one-off funding, not genuine ongoing financial capacity
findings.detail: The reserve reflects one-off funding transferred at year-end 2025/26, has been factored into 2026/27 financial strategy, and is expected to be substantially or fully committed during the year. The report explicitly states it does not represent ongoing capacity to absorb future pressures.
findings.matters: The improved financial position vs. prior recovery assumptions is partly artificial. Once this reserve depletes, structural pressures will re-emerge without further savings or service changes.
findings.figures: General Reserve £8.0m (one-off)
findings.quote: While the year-end position included a General Reserve of £8.0 million, this reflects one-off funding transferred into reserves at the end of 2025/26... it does not represent ongoing financial capacity to absorb future pressures.

findings.headline: Savings programme contains material risks that could unmask budget shortfall
findings.detail: The report explicitly states that some savings are assessed as being at risk of not being achieved in full, creating an emerging shortfall against the overall savings target. SLT are working to confirm deliverability and identify mitigating actions, with progress to be reported at the next IJB meeting. The overall budget balance depends on savings delivery.
findings.matters: If savings at risk materialise as failures, the reported £358k underspend forecast becomes a significant overspend, and the IJB will lack identified mitigations.
findings.figures: Overall forecast variance £358k (dependent on savings)
findings.quote: Delivery of the agreed savings programme remains essential to maintaining the balanced 2026/27 budget. Some savings are currently assessed as being at risk of not being achieved in full, creating an emerging shortfall against the overall savings target.

findings.headline: Council Social Care is forecast to overspend by £1.363m in 2026/27
findings.detail: Against a budget of £219.631m, Council Social Care spending is forecast at £220.994m. This is the largest and only material negative variance in the forecast position. The paper states the position will require ongoing close review as it is subject to change pending confirmation of assumptions.
findings.matters: A £1.4m overspend in a major service area masks underlying pressure and shows the overall budget balance is dependent on other areas staying underspent, creating fragility.
findings.figures: Council Social Care budget £219,631k, forecast £220,994k, variance (£1,363k)
findings.quote: Council – Social Care  219,631 220,994 (1,363)

findings.headline: Macmillan Nurses saving will deliver only 60% of the required £150,000
findings.detail: The original saving will 'not be delivered in the way originally intended'. An alternative has been identified that will deliver 'around 60% of the required saving', leaving a shortfall to be offset by the HSCP Sustainability Board.
findings.matters: Delivery mechanism failure on a specific service indicates risks beyond just financial pressure: there may be service provision concerns underlying the savings miss
findings.figures: £150,000 planned; ~£60,000 shortfall
findings.quote: This saving will not be delivered in the way originally intended. Alternative saving identified that will deliver around 60% of the required saving.

findings.headline: Around £2.3m of total planned savings (40% of the budget) face delivery risks or remain unconfirmed
findings.detail: Beyond the £700k RAS and £500k locum shortfalls, multiple other areas are at risk: Public Health (£85k), Estate Rationalisation (£316k), Macmillan Nurses (only 60% achievable as originally intended, shortfall ~£60k), Community hospital efficiency (£700k work ongoing), and three Older People services (£405k work ongoing).
findings.matters: This scale of unresolved savings delivery risk means the council's budget position is materially uncertain, requiring alternative savings that do not yet appear to be identified
findings.figures: £5,702,500 total planned; £2,300,000+ at risk or unconfirmed
findings.quote: The full saving is unlikely to be achieved in this financial year. The HSCP Sustainability Board are identifying alternative savings to offset the remainder.

findings.headline: Locum spend saving of £500,000 will not be delivered this financial year
findings.detail: The paper explicitly flags this saving as 'unlikely to be achieved in this financial year', requiring the HSCP Sustainability Board to identify alternative savings to offset the shortfall.
findings.matters: Another £500k shortfall adds to the budget pressure and means staffing costs in health and social care will run higher than planned
findings.quote: This saving is unlikely to be achieved in this financial year. The HSCP Sustainability Board are identifying alternative savings to offset

findings.headline: Learning Disability and Mental Health RAS savings of £700,000 cannot be achieved
findings.detail: The paper states the planned £700,000 saving from the review of resource allocation cannot be achieved. This was expected to be partially offset by Commissioning for Outcomes savings, but that is 'no longer possible'. The HSCP Sustainability Board must find alternative savings to cover the gap.
findings.matters: A £700,000 shortfall in a major service area creates a direct budget pressure that must be resolved or absorbed
findings.quote: With the majority of packages now reviewed the total savings planned cannot be achieved from this work.

findings.headline: £1.55m of agreed savings at risk, with only 5.2% achieved in Q1
findings.detail: Of £3.951m in total agreed savings, £1.550m are flagged as amber risk with £0.450m specifically unlikely to be achieved this year. Only £0.204m (5.2% of target) has been realised to date, suggesting savings delivery will need rapid acceleration to avoid widening the forecast deficit.
findings.matters: If at-risk savings do not materialise, the reported overspend will worsen and budget delivery becomes uncertain.
findings.figures: £3.951m total savings agreed; £1.550m amber risk; £0.450m at risk of non-delivery; £0.204m achieved (5.2%)
findings.quote: There is currently one saving (Amber) £1.550m, reported at risk of not being achieved in full this financial year. £1.100m forecast on target, £0.450m at risk

findings.headline: Q1 forecast overspend of £0.763m driven by school premises cost pressures
findings.detail: The committee is forecasting a full-year overspend of £0.763m driven primarily by increased school premises costs from rates and refuse collection charges (£0.603m) and unallocated savings (£0.450m). These pressures are partly offset by PPP/PFI unitary charge retentions of £200k and staffing underspends.
findings.matters: An active overspend forecast in Q1 signals budget control issues and ongoing cost pressures that may persist through the year.
findings.figures: £0.763m overspend; £0.603m rates and refuse; £0.450m unallocated savings
findings.quote: At this stage in the financial year, the functions within the remit of Education & Children's Services Committee are forecasting to be £0.763m over budget.

findings.headline: Grant-funded capital works at risk from late funding confirmation and claim delays
findings.detail: External grant funding is sometimes not confirmed until well into the financial year. Grant claim deadlines are a constraint on works delivery. Non-compliance with grant conditions or delays in claims could leave expenditure unfunded, creating a funding gap.
findings.matters: Late grant confirmation can force re-phasing of capital works, delaying service benefits. Unfunded expenditure—if claims are rejected or conditional funding is lost—would require the council to fund works from its own resources.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Some grant funding is not confirmed until well into the financial year, which can hinder the ability to undertake the works being funded by the end of the financial year.

findings.headline: Core service costs exposed to inflation and weather-driven demand across roads, maintenance and landscape operations
findings.detail: Roads maintenance, winter maintenance, landscape services and quarries all face acknowledged exposure to weather-related demand spikes, contract inflation, staffing pressures and materials costs. These are described as ongoing operational exposures requiring 'continued monitoring'.
findings.matters: These are essential services where cost inflation directly erodes the budget. An unexpectedly harsh winter or sustained inflation beyond current forecasts could break the on-budget position.
findings.figures: No quantum disclosed
findings.quote: Roads maintenance, winter maintenance, landscape services and quarries, as well as other services, remain exposed to weather-related demand, contract inflation, staffing pressures and materials costs.

findings.headline: Waste plant revenue exposed to external volatility in multiple dimensions
findings.detail: The Energy from Waste facility's financial performance depends on waste tonnage, electricity prices, gate fees, generation output and plant availability—factors largely outside council control. The paper explicitly states that changes to these assumptions could affect the full-year forecast.
findings.matters: This is often a material revenue stream for councils. Volatility here directly threatens budget assumptions and may force in-year reforecasting or require contingency action.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this report
findings.quote: Financial performance is sensitive to waste tonnage, gate fees, electricity prices, generation output and plant availability. Changes in these assumptions could affect the full-year forecast.

findings.headline: 98% of planned revenue savings not yet realised by end of Q1
findings.detail: The council approved £2.484m in savings for Infrastructure Services this year. By the end of June, only £0.061m (2.5%) has been achieved. The remaining £2.423m (97.5%) is categorised as 'on track', meaning the delivery is still entirely ahead. Realisation of these savings is essential to maintain the stated on-budget position.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether budgeted savings will actually materialise. With such early-stage delivery across 75% of the remaining year, implementation delays could quickly become a budget pressure.
findings.figures: £2.484m total savings target; £0.061m achieved (2.5%); £2.423m on track (97.5%)
findings.quote: Savings achieved to date (Complete): £0.061m (2.5% of target). Savings on track to being achieved (Green): £2.423m (97.5% of target)

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Internal Audit Update Report
findings.headline: Three major-rated audit recommendations extended beyond original implementation deadlines, indicating wider execution backlog
findings.detail: Originally 20 audit recommendations were due as of 31 May 2026 (four rated major, sixteen moderate). Seven were closed; thirteen remain outstanding (three major, ten moderate), with major items extended into August–September.
findings.matters: Extended deadlines on major audit findings suggest the council is managing more issues than it can resolve on schedule, indicating constrained management capacity for remediating control environment gaps.
findings.figures: 20 recommendations due 31 May 2026; 7 closed (1 major, 6 moderate); 13 outstanding (3 major, 10 moderate); three major recommendations extended 3–4 months
findings.quote: As at 31 May 2026 (the baseline for our exercise), 20 audit recommendations were due and outstanding: Four rated as Major, 16 rated as Moderate.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Internal Audit Update Report
findings.headline: Children's residential care budget grew 6.2% year-on-year with multiple control gaps in medication, payroll, and purchasing
findings.detail: Children's homes budget increased from £3.315m (2024/25 outturn) to £3.520m (2025/26). The audit identified control weaknesses requiring enhancement in medication control, payment processing, young people's expenses, timesheet approval, and purchase card use.
findings.matters: Significant budget escalation coupled with documented control environment gaps indicates unmanaged cost pressures without proportionate control strengthening, relevant to budget forecasting and financial risk.
findings.figures: 2025/26 budget £3.520m vs 2024/25 outturn £3.315m; increase of £205k (6.2%); operates 4 homes with 19 beds
findings.quote: The related Children – Residential Care Budget for 2025/26 is £3.520m (2024/25 outturn £3.315m).

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Internal Audit Update Report
findings.headline: Integration Joint Board flagged for financial sustainability and budget monitoring weaknesses in strategic governance audit
findings.detail: IJB governance review identified areas requiring further work on financial management and sustainability, budget monitoring, and risk management. These gaps formed part of a broad strategic-level audit designed to assess the framework of control.
findings.matters: IJB financial sustainability concerns indicate partnership viability risk and may reflect underlying budget pressures or delivery model challenges in health and social care services.
findings.figures: IJB assessment: MODERATE risk, REASONABLE assurance; eight audit recommendation areas identified
findings.quote: However, areas where further work is required to reinforce or improve assurance over governance have been identified as part of the audit including: Governance Framework, Risk Management, Performance Reporting, Financial Management and Sustainability, Budget Monitoring, Asset and Resource Management, and Information Governance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Internal Audit Update Report
findings.headline: Teachers payroll control improvements stalled by HR staffing attrition; four major recommendations extended from April to September
findings.detail: Documented weaknesses in payroll controls (missing supporting details, combined changes, insufficient evidence review) remain unresolved. Management attributed the delay to 'other priorities and attrition within the Team', indicating staffing loss in the payroll function.
findings.matters: Payroll control failures directly threaten financial accuracy; staffing attrition in the payroll function is a leading indicator of HR stability risk and operational control deterioration.
findings.figures: Four payroll recommendations: originally due April–May 2026, extended to September 2026; all marked In Progress
findings.quote: Management discussed the recommendation with Internal Audit, noting progress but not able to close off due to other priorities and attrition within the Team. Extended to allow for completion.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Internal Audit Update Report
findings.headline: Museums service rated MAJOR risk with LIMITED assurance; staff unable to progress mandatory control improvements due to competing priorities
findings.detail: Three accredited museums (budget £779k, 9.5 FTE) are failing to maintain compliance with accreditation standards. Collections documentation, loan management, preservation, and emergency plans all have documented gaps. Staff report slow progress on improvements due to workload constraints.
findings.matters: A MAJOR rated service failure in a delivered council function indicates insufficient operational capacity to maintain statutory compliance, with risks of loss, theft, and reputational damage.
findings.figures: Museums budget 2026/27 £779k (2025/26 outturn £788k); Arbuthnot Museum closed 2020, replacement museum scheduled 2028
findings.quote: Staff are reporting that progress has been slow addressing these issues due to competing priorities, and as noted throughout the report, risks to degradation, loss, and theft of items; financial loss; ineffective emergency response; and reputational damage could be mitigated further.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A – Internal Audit Update Report
findings.headline: Place Strategy has no delivery plan in place 15 months after council approval, rated MAJOR risk with LIMITED assurance
findings.detail: The Place Strategy was approved June 2024 but Place plans—the mechanism to translate strategy into deliverable action—remain largely undeveloped. This creates governance gaps: no SMART delivery plan, inconsistent officer oversight, and limited member scrutiny.
findings.matters: A major strategic initiative inoperable 15 months after approval indicates governance and programme management failures at the strategic level, raising questions about the council's ability to deliver transformation.
findings.figures: Place Strategy approved 27 June 2024; core delivery mechanism (Place plans) not in place
findings.quote: However, the Place Strategy is not yet operating as intended because Place plans, which are the primary mechanism for translating strategic intent into deliverable, Place based action, are largely not in place.

findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation contingency reduced while demand may remain uncertain
findings.detail: Private let deficit funding for temporary accommodation has been removed (£30k of the £100k homelessness saving) as the council has moved off RSL-leased properties to using its own stock. However, the paper explicitly notes a £30k contingency is being retained in case the council needs to lease properties again for particular needs.
findings.matters: The contingency cushion suggests the council recognises demand for emergency accommodation leasing may still arise; this is a demand-driven budget that could come under pressure.
findings.figures: £100,000 total saving; £30,000 retained as contingency for potential future leasing
findings.quote: The budget saving proposed is £30k which will leave a contingency should we require to lease properties which we cannot supply within our own stock in cases of requirements for particular needs.

findings.headline: Material income-generation savings are dependent on consultation approval and market conditions
findings.detail: £175k of the Sport and Physical Activity venues saving depends on reducing concessionary discounts for leisure activities, which is explicitly subject to consultation and committee approval. A further £491k assumes continued surplus from improved operational performance.
findings.matters: Income-dependent savings are vulnerable to demand fluctuations and approval delays; the council may need to find alternative cuts if these do not materialise.
findings.figures: £175,000 subject to consultation approval; £491,310 dependent on operational surplus
findings.quote: Income will be generated through changes to concessionary discounts for leisure activities. This would affect some users and is subject to consultation and committee approval.

findings.headline: Capital From Current Revenue reclassification estimate increased by £1m (43% above initial projection)
findings.detail: The council initially anticipated £2.5m could be reclassified from revenue to capital in 2026/27, but revised this upward to £3.5m after further analysis of roads maintenance expenditure. This suggests the council is relying more on accounting reclassification to reduce the apparent revenue deficit.
findings.matters: Revenue-to-capital reclassification is typically a one-off adjustment and can mask deteriorating underlying revenue position. A lender would want to understand whether the council is increasingly dependent on this mechanism.
findings.figures: Revised from £2.5m to £3.5m; £1m of the £9.25m total savings plan depends on CFCR
findings.quote: It was initially anticipated that expenditure eligible to be reclassified as capital through Capital From Current Revenue (CFCR) in 2026/27 would be around £2.5 million. However, following further detailed analysis of qualifying Roads Maintenance expenditure, this estimate has been revised to £3.5 million.

findings.headline: Council explicitly flags financial risk on vacancy-based savings if recruitment trends change
findings.detail: Two separate savings proposals (Community Learning £220k, Instrumental Music £110k) acknowledge they rely on historic vacancy management patterns and explicitly warn that if staffing recruitment trends do not continue, additional disinvestment measures may be required. The council is betting on vacancies staying high.
findings.matters: Vacancy management is inherently fragile as a savings mechanism—if the council needs to recruit, these savings evaporate, forcing real cuts elsewhere to meet budget targets.
findings.quote: However, this approach carries a financial risk, and if historic staffing trends do not continue, additional disinvestment measures may be required to manage the resulting budget pressure.

findings.headline: Difficult reallocation and disinvestment decisions still pending; recovery pace depends on urgency
findings.detail: The register identifies that the council has not yet made hard decisions to reallocate resources away from lower-priority or legacy activities. It states: 'Work is continuing...to challenge legacy spending patterns, prioritise investment, and identify where disinvestment or redesign is required.' The register concludes: 'This remains a significant strategic risk as the pace of financial recovery depends on timely decisions to redirect limited revenue, workforce and capital capacity.'
findings.matters: Lack of urgency on reallocation and disinvestment indicates the council is not yet taking the difficult decisions needed to close the structural gap. This suggests the recovery timeline is uncertain and dependent on future action, not current trajectory.
findings.figures: Risk score 20; residual risk 15
findings.quote: This remains a significant strategic risk as the pace of financial recovery depends on timely decisions to redirect limited revenue, workforce and capital capacity to the areas of greatest impact.

findings.headline: Integration Joint Board (health and social care) continues to draw on council reserves despite reported improvement
findings.detail: The IJB reported an improved position for 2025/26, resulting in a reduced draw on council reserves. However, the register explicitly states: 'There continues to be challenges over the medium term.' This indicates ongoing structural pressures in delegated health and social care services that will require continued reserve drawdown or additional council funding contributions.
findings.matters: Health and social care demand is growing and is largely outside council control. If the IJB cannot contain pressures, the council faces either recurring reserve depletion or service redesign that may increase statutory duty costs elsewhere.
findings.figures: Risk score 20; residual risk 15
findings.quote: The IJB has reported an improved position for 2025/26, resulting in the draw down form Council reserves being less than was set aside as part of the budget. There continues to be challenges over the medium term.

findings.headline: Capital programme being actively scaled back due to inflation and cost pressures
findings.detail: The council is managing capital inflation not through additional funding but through service delivery trade-offs: reducing project scope and specification, delivering fewer outputs, reprofiling works to later years, and reprioritising activity. The risk register identifies global geopolitical volatility in fuel, energy, materials, and transport creating transmission risk to capital plans, particularly for construction-intensive programmes and infrastructure schemes.
findings.matters: Deferred capital works accumulate. Infrastructure neglect creates future emergency costs and service failure; IT infrastructure deferral increases cyber-security risk; road and asset backlogs worsen over time.
findings.figures: Risk score 20 (updated to 16 residual); capital plan affordability identified as core affordability risk
findings.quote: In the absence of additional funding capacity, services are managing inflation almost entirely through delivery trade-offs - reducing scope/specification, delivering fewer outputs, reprofiling works to later years, and reprioritising activity within rolling programmes.

findings.headline: Council relying on one-off reserves and vacancy savings rather than recurring savings
findings.detail: The register explicitly identifies that improvements in the 2025/26 outturn used non-recurring funding sources (reserves, one-off savings, temporary grants, vacancy management). The register warns this creates a future budget gap and reduces reserves, with a stated need to "deliver recurring savings" that has not yet been met.
findings.matters: Reserves are not a sustainable funding source. A council drawing on them to balance annual budgets will exhaust them and face forced spending cuts or covenant breach.
findings.figures: Risk score 20; residual risk 12
findings.quote: these are one-off in nature. There remains a need to deliver recurring savings.

findings.headline: Structural budget gap persists despite improved 2025/26 outturn
findings.detail: The council achieved an improved outturn in 2025/26, but explicitly states this resulted from non-recurring factors, not underlying improvement. The risk register confirms the structural gap—where recurring expenditure exceeds sustainable recurring funding—remains unresolved and is expected to grow due to increasing demand, inflation, and constrained government funding.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether improved numbers reflect sustainable change or temporary measures. A council masking a structural gap with one-offs will face a sharper cliff when those measures end.
findings.figures: Risk score 25 (high); residual risk 16 after controls
findings.quote: While the 2025/26 draft outturn is an improved position, this has been achieved as a result of a number of non-recurring factors which has allowed the Council to take a planned, multi-year approach to strengthen financial resilience, rather than assume sustained improvement in the underlying position. The structural budget gap remains.

findings.headline: Non-recurring items and favourable timing masked underlying budget pressures; year-end position not sustainable
findings.detail: The council explicitly states: 'a number of the movements contributing to the year-end position are non-recurring or relate to the timing of expenditure and income. The improved outturn should therefore be applied on a prudent basis to strengthen the Council's financial resilience and address known risks carried into 2026/27, rather than be interpreted as a full resolution of the underlying financial pressures.' Favourable movements included lower winter maintenance (weather dependent), slippage in demolition, and one-off property fee income.
findings.matters: The £7.776m under-budget headline result is misleading. The council itself signals this is not sustainable and driven partly by items that will not recur (one-off income, timing slippage, better-than-expected winter). A lender needs to look through the headline to the structural position, which remains under pressure.
findings.figures: £7.776m gross under-budget, but reduced to £0.068m after proposed reserve transfers (£7.708m).
findings.quote: Notwithstanding this improvement, it is important to recognise that a number of the movements contributing to the year-end position are non-recurring or relate to the timing of expenditure and income. The improved outturn should therefore be applied on a prudent basis to strengthen the Council's financial resilience and address known risks carried into 2026/27, rather than be interpreted as a full resolution of the underlying financial pressures.

findings.headline: Energy from Waste legal case with contractor remains unresolved; £2.488m bond set aside as contingent protection
findings.detail: The council notes it 'anticipated potential additional cost pressures pending conclusion of the legal case with the contractor'. It has ringfenced £2.488m of bond income received 'to mitigate any future year pressures arising from the procurement of a replacement contract'. The council also holds a separate asset decommissioning provision of £9.514m total (including £1.878m for Energy from Waste plant decommissioning). This represents a significant unresolved liability.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility of material litigation and contingent liabilities that could crystallise into future costs. An unresolved contractor dispute plus £9.5m decommissioning provision signals this is a material long-term financial exposure with uncertain timing and final cost.
findings.figures: £2.488m bond monies earmarked; £9.514m total asset decommissioning provision (including £1.878m for EfW plant); legal case ongoing
findings.quote: pending conclusion of the legal case with the contractor. The Council's share of the bond received (£2.488m) has been earmarked within reserves to mitigate any future year pressures arising from the procurement of a replacement contract.

findings.headline: External borrowing deferred in 2025/26 must be secured in early 2026/27 to maintain liquidity
findings.detail: Capital financing charges were £6.075m under budget due to 'ability to defer external borrowing as a result of lower capital expenditure and higher cash balances during the year'. However, the report explicitly states: 'While this has supported the in-year revenue position, it places pressure on future years, as borrowing to support the approved Capital Plan has been deferred rather than avoided. New borrowing will require to be secured in early 2026/27 to maintain liquidity and support the timing of forecast cash flows.'
findings.matters: For a lender, this is material. The council did not reduce borrowing needs but postponed them. It must access credit markets in early 2026/27. This matters for understanding when the council will need to borrow and at what rates, and whether market conditions might constrain access.
findings.figures: £6.075m capital financing underspend in 2025/26; borrowing need deferred to early 2026/27
findings.quote: While this has supported the in-year revenue position, it places pressure on future years, as borrowing to support the approved Capital Plan has been deferred rather than avoided. New borrowing will require to be secured in early 2026/27 to maintain liquidity and support the timing of forecast cash flows.

findings.headline: Council Tax and general bad debt provisions increased by £3.6m following external audit challenge on collection assumptions
findings.detail: Bad debt provisions for Council Tax increased from £17.128m to £19.755m (£2.627m increase), and General Debtors provision increased by £1.000m. The report explicitly states this followed 'external audit comments on the optimism of the Council's previous assumptions' on collectability. This reduces reported income and signals collection risks or demographic changes affecting debt recovery.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in the council's core funding. Rising bad debt provisions suggest either collection challenges, increased number of uncollectable debts (poverty/vulnerability indicator), or prior over-optimism in forecasting. This strengthens the balance sheet but signals risk.
findings.figures: Council Tax provision increased £2.627m to £19.755m. General Debtors provision increased £1.000m to £4.087m. Total bad debt provision increase £3.6m.
findings.quote: A revised provision methodology was approved through the 2025/26 MTFS following external audit comments on the optimism of the Council's previous assumptions. Applying the revised methodology in 2025/26 has increased the General Debtors bad debt provision by £1.000m.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure slipped 31-32% across both General Services and HRA, driven by procurement, planning and utility constraints
findings.detail: General Services Capital Plan spent £65.485m against revised budget of £96.127m (£30.642m or 31.8% underspend). HRA Capital Plan spent £21.558m against £31.413m budget (£9.855m or 31.5% underspend). The council identifies slippage driven by 'procurement delays', 'planning and legal processes', 'supply chain constraints' and 'utility or environmental issues', with rephasing into 2026/27. This is not reduced scope but postponement, meaning capital and borrowing needs shift into future years.
findings.matters: Large, consistent capital slippage signals delivery capacity constraints or external barriers. This defers borrowing needs (a lender concern) and may indicate the council cannot deliver the capital programme as planned, which affects service resilience and asset condition.
findings.figures: General Services: £65.485m actual vs £96.127m revised budget (£30.642m underspend, 31.8%). HRA: £21.558m actual vs £31.413m budget (£9.855m underspend, 31.5%).
findings.quote: Actual expenditure on the General Services Capital Plan in 2025/26 was £65.485m, which is £30.642m below the revised budget of £96.127m and 31.8% lower than planned. This variance was driven mainly by slippage and rephasing of major projects rather than reductions in approved scope.

findings.headline: Out of Authority placement costs in Children's Services grew by £2.616m due to increased demand
findings.detail: Children's Services reported an over-budget position of £0.971m, primarily driven by higher Out of Authority (OoA) placement costs. The council faced £2.616m additional demand for OoA placements, which was only partially offset by under-budget positions in other areas (staff vacancies £0.408m, foster care £0.617m). This is demand-led spending with limited council control.
findings.matters: Demand-led cost pressures in children's social care are harder to control through efficiency and may indicate growing social need, demographic pressure, or complexity requiring sustained funding. A lender needs to know if this is a one-off or trend.
findings.figures: £2.616m additional OoA placement costs; Children's Services overall overspend £0.971m
findings.quote: Children's Services – reported an over-budget position of £0.971m, mainly due to higher Out of Authority placement costs arising from increased demand £2.616m

findings.headline: Savings targets missed: only 75% of £26.8m planned savings achieved
findings.detail: The Council approved savings of £26.819m for 2025/26 but delivered only £20.001m on a recurring basis (75%). Education and Children's Services missed £3.685m of savings; Infrastructure Services missed £2.485m. Unachieved savings were spread across staffing and transformation targets with no clear recurring budget line identified to permanently apply them.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's budget assumptions are reliable and whether announced savings will actually materialise. Missing 25% of a planned savings plan suggests budget pressures may be structural, not temporary.
findings.figures: £26.819m budgeted, £20.001m achieved, £6.818m not achieved. Education missed £3.685m; Infrastructure missed £2.485m.
findings.quote: The Council approved savings of £26.819m for 2025/26. £20.001m of savings have been achieved on a recurring basis (75%)

findings.paper_title: Roads and Infrastructure Capital Programmes of Work 2026-27
findings.headline: Using Current Financing from Current Revenue (CFCR) and Scottish Government grant reprofiling to fund capital works
findings.detail: £500,000 for resurfacing works will be funded from current revenue rather than capital budget. Scottish Government AWPR grant funding is being reprofiled to advance £500,000 into 2026-27 for specific road schemes. These mechanisms indicate the capital budget is insufficient for planned works.
findings.matters: Funding capital from revenue reduces operational flexibility; dependence on grant reprofiling creates timing and availability risks if external funding becomes unavailable.
findings.figures: £500,000 from CFCR for resurfacing; £500,000 AWPR funding advanced into 2026-27
findings.quote: It is intended to fund this capital expenditure from current revenue (CFCR). Similarly, it is proposed to reprofile the Scottish Government AWPR monies within the Capital Plan to advance £500,000 into 2026-27

findings.paper_title: Roads and Infrastructure Capital Programmes of Work 2026-27
findings.headline: Road network asset base growing through developer adoptions whilst maintenance funding remains constrained
findings.detail: The council notes that the statutory road network continues to expand as developers deliver schemes that are then adopted onto the council's assets, increasing maintenance obligations. This growth in assets occurs within a funding environment already described as below steady-state levels.
findings.matters: Growing asset base with constrained funding creates a structural squeeze that accelerates infrastructure deterioration and increases long-term financial liabilities.
findings.figures: No quantified adoption rate provided
findings.quote: the road network and all the related assets continue to grow as developments are adopted on to the Statutory List of Roads and become the Council's responsibility

findings.paper_title: Roads and Infrastructure Capital Programmes of Work 2026-27
findings.headline: Budget constraints forcing shift away from preventative maintenance toward reactive repairs, contradicting asset management best practice
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that constrained preventative spending forces increasing reliance on reactive maintenance to address road safety defects, which violates the principle that prevention is more effective and cost-efficient than cure. This reactive posture indicates the council is managing decline rather than maintaining infrastructure.
findings.matters: Reactive maintenance costs significantly more per unit than preventative work; this shift signals structural asset management failure and deepening financial pressures.
findings.figures: No quantified reactive vs preventative ratio provided
findings.quote: the need for reactive maintenance to address road safety defects will again increase. This balance between reactive maintenance and preventative maintenance, that sees us focusing on the former, goes against the accepted asset management principle that 'prevention is better than cure'.

findings.paper_title: Roads and Infrastructure Capital Programmes of Work 2026-27
findings.headline: Bridges capital spending cut by £4.7 million (61%) in a single year, from £7.7m to £3.0m
findings.detail: Bridges capital budget fell sharply from £7,735,000 in 2025-26 to £3,000,000 in 2026-27. The council maintains a £300,000 allocation for unplanned emergency repairs and climate adaptation, but total bridges maintenance investment has been significantly reduced.
findings.matters: A 61% year-on-year reduction in critical infrastructure maintenance indicates severe budget constraints and deferred maintenance that creates safety risks and future financial liabilities.

findings.paper_title: Roads and Infrastructure Capital Programmes of Work 2026-27
findings.headline: Council explicitly acknowledges 'managed decline' of the road network due to funding below steady-state levels
findings.detail: The council states that current funding for roads maintenance remains below what is needed to properly maintain the network, resulting in witnessed 'managed decline'. Whilst planned preventative maintenance is resuming, the percentage of the network receiving new or enhanced surfaces remains low. The shift toward reactive maintenance to address safety defects goes against established asset management practice.
findings.matters: A council unable to maintain its asset base to required standards creates future financial liabilities, signals structural budget stress, and indicates deteriorating infrastructure that could affect borrowing capacity and council viability.
findings.figures: Roads maintenance budget increased to £23,086,000 (2026-27) from £18,763,000 (2025-26), yet described as still below steady-state requirement
findings.quote: the current level of funding for roads maintenance remains well below steady state levels. As such, we continue to witness the managed decline of the road network.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial sustainability strategy remains under development
findings.detail: The statement references progress on developing a Medium-Term Financial Strategy and explicitly acknowledges that further work is required to embed financial sustainability over the medium term. This indicates planning is not yet complete or settled.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that a material service provider has a clear, forward financial plan; a strategy still in development suggests ongoing planning uncertainty and potential for future pressures.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: while improvement has been made, further work is required to embed financial sustainability over the medium term

findings.headline: The IJB remains in active financial recovery despite recent improvements
findings.detail: The governance statement acknowledges that financial arrangements have strengthened during 2025/26 and progress is being made on a Recovery Plan. However, it explicitly states that continued focus is required to sustain financial recovery and support longer-term financial sustainability, indicating the recovery is not yet complete.
findings.matters: The IJB (a partnership between Aberdeenshire Council and NHS Grampian) is a material service area; ongoing financial recovery indicates structural challenges that could affect the parent council's financial position and future borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Although arrangements have strengthened during 2025/26, continued focus is required to sustain financial recovery and support longer-term financial sustainability

findings.headline: Audit Scotland flags that IJBs across Scotland face a critical financial position with costs and demand rising faster than available resources.
findings.detail: Audit Scotland's February 2026 bulletin warns that costs and demand are rising faster than available resources across Scottish IJBs and partners are 'increasingly constrained in their ability to provide additional in-year support'. Aberdeenshire's report explicitly aligns its MTFS with this finding, stating these are not hypothetical risks but evidenced system-wide impacts.
findings.matters: Third-party validation that the IJB's problems are structural, not local mismanagement. It signals that financial pressures will persist and worsen, and that partner bailouts (the current stabilisation mechanism) may not be available indefinitely.
findings.figures: Audit Scotland February 2026 bulletin flagging IJBs across Scotland in 'critical financial position'
findings.quote: These updates also align with the national picture set out in Audit Scotland's February 2026 bulletin, which highlights that IJBs across Scotland are facing a critical financial position, with costs and demand rising faster than available resources and partners increasingly constrained in their ability to provide additional in-year support.

findings.headline: Social care has already been cut to the point where further savings risk service safety; health budgets must carry future savings burden.
findings.detail: Social care has 'already delivered significant savings in recent years' and has reached 'the point where further reductions could risk the safe delivery of essential services'. A 'greater proportion' of the rolling £6m annual savings target must therefore come from health budgets. The savings well is running dry in the part of the business where safety is non-negotiable.
findings.matters: If health now carries the savings burden and social care cannot cut further without safety compromise, the partnership has limited room to respond to the next crisis. Audit Scotland's February 2026 bulletin warns that IJBs across Scotland face a 'critical financial position'.
findings.figures: Rolling three-year savings requirement: approximately £6 million annually. 2026/27 savings proposals: £5.718m
findings.quote: social care budgets have already delivered significant savings in recent years, reaching the point where further reductions could risk the safe delivery of essential services. As a result, while savings for 2026/27 continue to be drawn from both health and social care, a greater proportion is expected to come from the health element of the budget

findings.headline: Both funding partners injected emergency additional funding on top of statutory contributions to prevent 2026/27 deficit.
findings.detail: Aberdeenshire Council added £6.5m above statutory contributions plus £8m for Real Living Wage and National Care Home Contract costs. NHS Grampian confirmed the full deficit funding request is 'fully incorporated' into its draft financial plan, pending Board approval. These are emergency allocations made specifically to balance the budget.
findings.matters: This is not routine budget-setting. Partners had to decide whether to bail out the IJB for a second consecutive year. A lender would see this as evidence that statutory funding is insufficient and future support depends on partner discretion.
findings.figures: Aberdeenshire Council additional funding: £6.5m above statutory + £8m for care costs. Total Agreed Additional Partner Funding: £13.818m
findings.quote: This included an additional £6.5 million to the Integration Joint Board above statutory contributions, alongside £8 million to meet increased costs associated with the Real Living Wage and the National Care Home Contract.

findings.headline: Aberdeenshire is forecasting a £9.7 million underlying overspend in 2025/26 even after absorbing £17.2 million in partner bailout funding.
findings.detail: The year-to-date position (end January 2026) shows a £7.9m underbudget, but this masks an underlying overspend of £9.7m once partner underwriting is accounted for. The full-year forecast projects a £7.4m underbudget, yet £9.7m of the available £17.2m partner rescue funding is 'currently expected to be required'. This reveals systematic overspending that only partner bailouts conceal.
findings.matters: The IJB cannot live within its budget and requires ongoing partner rescue funding to survive. The fact that £9.7m of partner support is 'currently expected to be required' indicates this is structural, not one-off.
findings.figures: Underlying overspend 2025/26: £9.732 million. Available partner underwriting: £17.155 million. Current forecast year-end underbudget: £7.423m
findings.quote: Because the budget assumed £17.155 million of partner underwriting, this translates to an underlying overspend of £9.732 million, meaning that £9.732 million of the available underwriting is currently expected to be required.

findings.headline: A Financial Recovery Plan implemented in 2025/26 due to uncontrollable overspends is only now being considered for closure.
findings.detail: The IJB implemented a formal Recovery Plan in 2025/26 because forecast overspends could not be managed through normal controls. This applied strengthened governance, enhanced reporting, and tighter spending controls. Management is now considering closure, but only following discussions with statutory officers and partners, and explicitly stating closure 'does not indicate the removal of financial risk'.
findings.matters: A Recovery Plan signals an organisation lost financial control and required exceptional intervention. That it took one year to stabilise and closure is merely 'being considered' indicates the underlying pressures remain unresolved.
findings.figures: Recovery Plan implemented 2025/26; closure status to be decided
findings.quote: A Financial Recovery Plan was implemented in 2025/26 under sections 12.6 and 12.7 of the Integration Scheme due to forecast overspends that could not be managed through normal controls.

findings.headline: The IJB enters 2026/27 with zero reserves and no confirmed funding beyond this year.
findings.detail: Despite a nominally balanced 2026/27 budget, the IJB will have no available reserves. Funding partners have only confirmed support for 2026/27; neither NHS Grampian nor Aberdeenshire Council has confirmed allocations for years beyond. This means the partnership is entirely dependent on continued discretionary partner support.
findings.matters: Zero reserves remove any buffer against demand spikes, price inflation, or service pressures. A lender would view reliance on unconfirmed future discretionary funding as a structural sustainability risk.
findings.figures: No reserves for 2026/27; funding confirmed 2026/27 only
findings.quote: The IJB will enter 2026/27 with no available reserves. This confirmation relates to the 2026/27 financial year only. Neither NHS Grampian nor Aberdeenshire Council has confirmed funding allocations for the IJB beyond this period.

findings.paper_title: Audited Annual Accounts and Annual Audit Report 2024/25 for Aberdeenshire Council
findings.headline: Council failed to meet 30 September audit completion deadline due to delays in asset valuations
findings.detail: Aberdeenshire did not meet the non-statutory 30 September 2025 audit completion target for the 2024/25 accounts. The delay was caused by delays in obtaining asset valuations for the balance sheet. Officers are reviewing processes to address this for 2025/26, but the missed deadline indicates process issues in asset management and financial reporting procedures.
findings.matters: Missed audit deadlines can indicate weakened financial controls, asset management issues, or delays in identifying problems; timely reporting is important for lender confidence
findings.figures: Non-statutory deadline of 30 September 2025; not achieved
findings.quote: Aberdeenshire has not met this target deadline for 2024/25. This is due to delays in obtaining asset valuations which form part of the Balance Sheet.

findings.paper_title: Audited Annual Accounts and Annual Audit Report 2024/25 for Aberdeenshire Council
findings.headline: Material accounting errors in pensions and PFI liabilities required adjustments during audit process
findings.detail: The council's actuaries identified an error in pension benefits paid figures in the IAS 19 schedules in early December 2025. Separately, the auditor's technical PFI team identified an error in PFI liability remeasurement methodology under the new IFRS 16 standard. Both required adjustments to the financial statements. While these adjustments had no impact on usable reserves, the errors indicate potential gaps in the council's financial controls and accounting processes.
findings.matters: Material accounting errors, even when corrected, suggest control weaknesses that could mask other financial issues; lenders need confidence in financial reporting reliability
findings.figures: No quantified impact stated; no impact on usable reserves
findings.quote: During this process, Grant Thornton's technical PFI team identified an error in the remeasurement methodology, resulting in an adjustment to the financial statements

findings.paper_title: Audited Annual Accounts and Annual Audit Report 2024/25 for Aberdeenshire Council
findings.headline: External auditor concluded there is significant risk to council's financial sustainability and ability to achieve budgets and savings plans
findings.detail: The auditor has explicitly identified a significant risk in respect of financial sustainability, and a significant risk regarding the council's ability to set and achieve realistic budgets and savings plans. This is stated as part of the auditor's wider-scope audit conclusions beyond the accounts themselves. Management has accepted the recommendations but the auditor's risk assessment indicates ongoing material concerns about financial viability and planning.
findings.matters: Lenders require confidence that a council can sustain service delivery and meet financial obligations; auditor-identified significant risks to financial sustainability are a critical indicator of creditworthiness and ability to service borrowing
findings.figures: No specific figures; auditor's risk assessment finding
findings.quote: The External Auditor has concluded that there remains a significant risk in respect of financial sustainability, and that the risk in relation to setting achievable budgets and savings plans is significant.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10A - Statement of All Council Reserves
findings.headline: Risk & Inflation Reserve drawn down by £3.7m in first year of forecast period
findings.detail: The Risk & Inflation Reserve is forecast to decline from £15,658k at April 2025 to £11,981k by March 2026, then stabilize at £12,432k from April 2026 onwards. The £3.7m drawdown in the first year is substantial.
findings.matters: Significant drawdown of the inflation buffer reserve indicates the council is absorbing cost pressures through reserve depletion rather than budget action, reducing its protection against future cost inflation.
findings.quote: Risk & Inflation Reserve (15,658) (11,981) (12,432)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10A - Statement of All Council Reserves
findings.headline: Integration Joint Board shortfall reserve of £7.4m will be completely depleted by April 2026
findings.detail: The Underwrite IJB Shortfall reserve is forecast to fall from £7,377k at April 2025 to zero by April 2026 and remain at zero thereafter. This reserve supports health and social care budget pressures through the Integration Joint Board, but the council is forecasting no replacement funding after April 2026.
findings.matters: After April 2026, the council has no dedicated reserve to absorb health and social care budget pressures; any future IJB shortfalls will directly impact the general fund or force service reductions.
findings.figures: (7,377) to 0 by April 2026
findings.quote: Underwrite IJB Shortfall (7,377) (2,000) 0 0 0 0 0

findings.paper_title: Appendix 10A - Statement of All Council Reserves
findings.headline: General Fund Balance forecast to decline from £9m to £29m over five years
findings.detail: The council's General Fund Balance is planned to decline from £9,000k at April 2025 to £29,000k by April 2030, a reduction of £20m. This is the council's main working reserve and is declining steadily across the forecast period.
findings.matters: Declining working balances indicate the council is using accumulated reserves to manage its budget; once exhausted, this significantly impacts financial resilience and will likely require increased borrowing or service reductions.
findings.figures: (9,000) declining to (29,000)

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget does not rely on reserves to balance, signalling sustainable approach
findings.detail: Explicitly, the Council will not use reserves to achieve balance for 2026/27. Instead, reserves are being maintained and increased to manage risk and volatility, while balance is achieved through structural solutions. This rules out reserve drawdown as a mitigation option.
findings.matters: Indicates the Council is not masking structural problems with one-time measures; important for lenders assessing whether financial strategy is credible and sustainable rather than dependent on reducing buffer reserves
findings.figures: No figures provided
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget does not rely on reserves to achieve balance

findings.headline: Adult social care demand surge from demographic change is the single primary financial driver
findings.detail: Population aged 65+ increasing sharply with declining healthy life expectancy and growing demand for adult social care in both volume and complexity. The Council is prioritising investment here, but notes these demographic trends cannot be managed through efficiencies alone and will shape resource allocation throughout the MTFS period.
findings.matters: Creates multi-year cost growth outpacing funding; structural demographic pressure on service demand and financial sustainability that will not ease and forces ongoing difficult choices between service areas
findings.figures: Population 65+ increasing sharply; healthy life expectancy declining; working-age population will contract
findings.quote: Demand for adult social care will grow in both volume and complexity

findings.headline: £293m medium-term borrowing requirement identified but capital investment deliberately constrained
findings.detail: The MTFS identifies a £293m borrowing need over the medium term. However, the Council is explicitly limiting capital because new borrowing would lock in long-term financing costs at a time of revenue pressure and higher interest rates. Capital decisions will prioritise statutory delivery and asset rationalisation over asset preservation.
findings.matters: Material debt requirement, but council is conscious of debt burden and protecting revenue flexibility; signals either capital underfunding or asset disinvestment ahead, which affects long-term service capacity
findings.figures: £293m borrowing requirement
findings.quote: Borrowing decisions taken now would lock in long-term financing costs, reducing flexibility in future budgets

findings.headline: Structural funding gap cannot be resolved through efficiencies alone; requires disinvestment
findings.detail: The Council faces a structural and recurring funding gap across the MTFS period that exceeds funding growth. Even with the 2026/27 uplift, unavoidable cost pressures (pay, inflation, policy commitments) consume the funding, creating a gap that persists. Disinvestment proposals of £9.254m are planned for 2026/27 as deliberate prioritisation decisions, not contingency.
findings.matters: Signals multi-year structural pressure requiring ongoing service reduction, not one-time efficiency gains; critical for lenders assessing whether the council's position is cyclical or permanent
findings.figures: £9.254m disinvestment for 2026/27; cumulative funding gap across 2026/27-2030/31
findings.quote: the Council's financial challenge remains structural rather than cyclical and requires a combination of service reprioritisation, transformation and increases in Council Tax to maintain financial balance

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5A - Treasury Management and Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Council deliberately under-borrowing, using reserves to delay borrowing on assumption rates will fall
findings.detail: Aberdeenshire is maintaining a £114m under-borrowed position, choosing not to match its borrowing need with loan debt and instead drawing down reserves to fund capital spending. This strategy rests entirely on the assumption that medium and long-term borrowing rates will fall. If rates remain elevated or rise, the council faces forced borrowing at worse rates while reserves are depleted.
findings.matters: A lender must understand this deliberate reserve depletion and the strength of the rate-fall assumption. Strategy failure leaves the council with eroded buffers and forced borrowing at unfavorable terms.
findings.figures: Under-borrowing (net treasury position): £981.861m deficit (Jan 2026). External debt £1,020.8m vs CFR £1,378.3m forecast 2026/27.
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. This strategy is prudent as medium and longer dated borrowing rates are expected to fall from their current levels.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5A - Treasury Management and Investment Strategy
findings.headline: HRA financing costs rising to 26.9% of revenue by 2028/29, squeezing housing service headroom
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account financing costs (debt service) are projected to grow from 23.3% to 26.9% of net housing revenue over the forecast period. This shows housing services becoming progressively more constrained by debt, with less room to absorb shocks or additional capital needs without cutting services or reserves.
findings.matters: Rising financing ratios in HRA indicate tightening revenue headroom and increased vulnerability to any disruption in rental income or need for emergency capital spending. For a lender, this trend signals decreasing financial flexibility in a major service.
findings.quote: HRA 23.3% 24.1% 25.0% 26.9% (from Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream table, 2025/26 through 2028/29 estimates)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 5A - Treasury Management and Investment Strategy
findings.headline: Capital expenditure peaks at £163.9m in 2027/28, requiring £114.8m net borrowing that single year
findings.detail: The council's capital spending is forecast to reach £163.9m in 2027/28 (its peak), creating a £114.8m financing gap that year. This represents a material spike from £134.7m and £87.1m borrowing need in the surrounding years, concentrating refinancing risk into one year when market conditions and the council's debt capacity could constrain options.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether the council can finance this peak without stress and whether underlying revenue can sustain the resulting debt service. Concentrated borrowing needs reduce negotiating power and increase refinancing risk.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure 2027/28: £163.922m. Net financing need 2027/28: £114.828m. Capital Financing Requirement grows from £1,308.472m (2025/26) to £1,528.647m (2028/29).
findings.quote: Capital expenditure 2027/28 Estimate £m 163.922. Net financing need for the year 2027/28 Estimate 114.828.

findings.paper_title: Aberdeenshire Council and Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-31
findings.headline: Budget balance depends on delivery of proposed staff reductions
findings.detail: The council states that achieving the 2026/27 budget 'may necessitate staff reductions in some cases' but does not quantify the numbers or value of proposed cuts in the main report. Implementation will depend on consultation with unions and employees. If savings do not materialise or are delayed, the budget will not balance.
findings.matters: Staffing savings built into the budget but not yet detailed creates execution risk; employment law and union negotiations can delay or prevent savings from landing on schedule.
findings.figures: Specific numbers and values of proposed reductions not given in main budget report
findings.quote: The proposed budget may necessitate staff reductions in some cases to achieve the agreed efficiencies and policy changes. The impact on staffing due to service reductions and changes will be evaluated to minimise effects.

findings.paper_title: Aberdeenshire Council and Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-31
findings.headline: Transformation Reserve support to health and social care IJB will not be repaid
findings.detail: The council provided financial support to the Integration Joint Board (health and social care) from the Transformation Reserve in 2024/25. This support is now being written off and will not be repaid, effectively a permanent reduction in reserves. The council justified this as recognition of the IJB's improving financial position, but it remains subject to ongoing review.
findings.matters: A non-repayable draw on reserves reduces the council's financial resilience and signals the IJB may have had prior financial instability requiring council support, which is a shared governance risk.
findings.figures: Amount of support to IJB not quantified in main report
findings.quote: Agree that the financial support provided to the IJB from the Transformation Reserve in 2024/25 will not be repaid at this stage, in recognition of the improved financial stability, grip and control being demonstrated by the IJB, and the risk that repayment would undermine the sustainability of that position.

findings.paper_title: Aberdeenshire Council and Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-31
findings.headline: Transformation Reserve was under suspension and now requires tightened governance
findings.detail: The council had imposed a temporary suspension on use of its Transformation Reserve, which is now being lifted only under a 'strengthened governance approach' requiring evidence-based business cases. This signals prior loss of control over reserve drawdowns and suggests the council previously faced pressure to restrict access to this reserve.
findings.matters: A prior suspension of reserve access indicates the council had control issues managing transformation spending. Tightened governance now suggests the council recognises this risk.
findings.figures: N/A
findings.quote: Agree that the temporary suspension on the use of Transformation Reserve will be lifted and be replaced with a strengthened governance approach and accessed only where a clear, evidence based business case is approved, demonstrating transformational impact, affordability, deliverability and effective management of financial risk

findings.paper_title: Aberdeenshire Council and Housing Revenue Account Budget 2026-31
findings.headline: Council Tax increased by 10% in 2026/27, with 8% rise planned for 2027/28
findings.detail: A 10% Council Tax rise for 2026/27 is substantially higher than the typical 3–5% seen elsewhere. The subsequent 8% rise in 2027/28 signals the council is front-loading increases to address a near-term funding gap. This pattern usually indicates either deferred cost pressures or a structural revenue shortfall.
findings.matters: A 10% Council Tax rise is unusual and signals a significant budget gap not covered by other funding sources. For a lender, this raises questions about whether the council's cost base is sustainable relative to its funding.
findings.quote: Agree to increase Council Tax by 10% in 2026/27 (Band D, £1,686.04), and agree indicative increases of 8% in 2027/28, and 2.25% from years 2028/29 to 2030/31

findings.headline: Long-term HRA business plan is no longer considered affordable despite cost-saving actions
findings.detail: The council's 30-year housing business plan operates under a 40% affordability ceiling, restricting debt service to no more than 40p in every £1 of rental income. However, the document states the plan is no longer affordable in the longer term due to high interest rates, construction inflation, and the cost of meeting Scottish Government standards. Although Communities Committee agreed an action plan to improve viability that is delivering savings, these structural pressures remain a significant risk.
findings.matters: An HRA approaching affordability limits signals constrained investment capacity, potential for unsustainable rent increases, and difficulty servicing housing debt—all material concerns for lenders evaluating the council's overall financial resilience.
findings.figures: 40% affordability ceiling; £78.7m rental income (including 5% increase); £27.7m maintenance expenditure; £31.1m capital programme
findings.quote: the business plan is no longer considered affordable in the longer term. Following the HRA Business Plan review, Communities Committee agreed an action plan to improve the viability of the HRA. This is delivering savings, however ongoing pressures (such as high interest rates, construction inflation and investment required to meet Scottish Government standards) remain a significant risk to longer-term viability.

findings.headline: HRA New Build Programme temporarily paused pending outcome of HRA Business Plan review
findings.detail: As part of a review of the HRA Business Plan, the New Build Programme was temporarily paused to assess capacity across workstreams. This is a separate factor from external supply chain delays and suggests internal review of the HRA's financial capacity.
findings.matters: Pausing housing supply delivery raises questions about HRA financial sustainability and capacity, signalling potential stress in the HRA's position that warrants investigation
findings.figures: HRA capital budget £50.31m, actual £41.49m, underspend £8.82m
findings.quote: as a result of the review of the HRA Business Plan, the New Build Programme was temporarily paused to determine capacity across workstreams.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure came in £47m below budget—a 31% underspend—with major projects delayed by supply chain issues and contractor availability
findings.detail: General Fund capital spend was £60.60m against a £98.80m budget (38% underspend) and HRA capital was £41.49m against £50.31m budget (18% underspend). The total programme underspent by £47.02m. Major projects including Peterhead Community Campus & Levelling Up faced delays, and the Housing Improvement Plan slowed due to contractor labour constraints and material lead times.
findings.matters: A significant underspend indicates the council is struggling to deliver its capital programme on schedule, which raises questions about project delivery capability and may delay service improvements or economic impact
findings.figures: Total budget £149.11m, actual £102.09m, underspend £47.02m (31%); General Fund underspend £38.20m; HRA underspend £8.82m
findings.quote: Several programmes of works were delayed due to supply chain issues and revised start dates on major projects such as Peterhead Community Campus & Levelling Up. Other projects that faced delays were beyond the control of the Council, for example, the North East Integrated mortuary project.

findings.headline: HRA financing costs reached 19.97% of revenue, nearly 7 percentage points above the 13% budget
findings.detail: The HRA financing ratio significantly exceeded budget due to a shorter repayment period for loans fund advances and increased interest charges as the proportion of HRA debt outstanding increased. This represents a material variance in the cost of servicing HRA debt.
findings.matters: Unexpectedly high debt servicing costs in the HRA reduce financial headroom and signal pressure on the HRA's position, which is material to both the council's finances and potential lenders to the authority
findings.figures: 19.97% actual vs 13.00% budget; variance of 6.97 percentage points
findings.quote: Financing costs for HRA were higher than budget due to a combination of factors, including a shorter repayment period for loans fund advances compared to that originally budgeted and a variation in interest charges payable as the proportion of HRA debt outstanding increased.

news_drafts.headline: Staff capacity diverted to Museum of Aberdeenshire capital project is slowing resolution of audit findings
news_drafts.lead: Staff capacity constraints around a major capital project may indicate competing demand on management bandwidth, potentially affecting both project delivery and control framework oversight.

news_drafts.headline: 70% of loans out have expired agreements; 92% lack insurance documentation; 84% lack annual condition reports
news_drafts.lead: Uninsured loaned items and expired agreements create unmitigated financial and cultural loss risk; control failures mean items may be damaged, lost, or stolen with no recovery mechanism.

news_drafts.headline: Accreditation expires 31 August 2026 with re-submission due September 2026, while audit identified multiple gaps in required governance policies
news_drafts.lead: Loss of accreditation would damage council reputation, impact grant funding eligibility, and signal inability to meet professional standards; the tight timeline creates execution risk.
